verses.translation_literal: Of David. I will give thanks to you with all my heart; before gods I will make music to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David. With everything in me, with the whole of my heart, I give you thanks. And I will not whisper it: before the gods themselves, before the powers of the earth, I will lift my voice and make music to you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first word, לְדָוִד, is the superscription: 'of David', or 'to David', or 'for David'. The preposition does not tell us whether he wrote the psalm, sang it, or was the king for whom it was written. KJV's 'A Psalm of David' fixes the first reading and adds the word 'psalm', which is not in the Hebrew.

The heart (לֵב) in Hebrew is the seat of thought and will, not of emotion. 'With all my heart' means with undivided mind and intention, as Radak says (בכל דעתי ושכלי) and Meiri says (בכוונה שלימה). The two verbs are a pair: אוֹדְךָ is thanks said aloud, as a public acknowledgement, and אֲזַמְּרֶךָּ is thanks sung to an instrument. Ibn Ezra splits them: thanks in the hidden place of the heart, song in the open.

The hard word is אֱלֹהִים. KJV and the other four English versions write 'the gods', which a modern reader hears as other deities. Rashi takes it as the angels, and Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra take it as judges and the wise, who are called אֱלֹהִים in Ex 22:8 where the case 'comes before the elohim'. The Targum has 'before judges'. The stage picture is the same either way: David sings in front of an audience of the powerful, unashamed.

philological_notes.note: The plural noun that is the ordinary word for God (with a singular verb) and also for gods. Here it has no article and no verb, so it can mean gods, divine beings or judges. The commentaries read it as judges or the wise, citing Ex 22:8; Rashi reads angels.
The Piel of זמר means to make music, to sing to a stringed accompaniment. It is the verb that gives the word mizmor ('psalm'). The English 'sing praise' hides the musical sense.

verses.translation_literal: I will bow down toward the temple of your holiness, and I will give thanks to your name for your covenant loyalty and for your faithfulness; for you have made great over all your name your word.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will bow low, my face toward your holy house, and there give thanks to your name: for your steadfast love, and for your faithfulness that does not fail. For you have set your word higher than every name you bear, and made it greater than all.
verses.directors_commentary:
אֶשְׁתַּחֲוֶה is to bow down, to lie full length with the face to the ground, the posture of a subject before a king. KJV's 'worship' is a Latin-derived word for the same act. The destination is 'the hêkhal of your holiness', the temple or palace. Ibn Ezra rules out the heavens as too distant for 'bow toward', and says it means the place of the ark. Radak says the house that will hold the ark, and Meiri says the place of the divine presence; Malbim reads it as the heavenly palace. David is bowing toward a building that may not stand yet, which is worth keeping in mind for the staging.

חֶסֶד and אֱמֶת are the pair that describes God in covenant terms: חֶסֶד is loyalty to a bond, and אֱמֶת is reliability, that the promise stands. KJV's 'lovingkindness' makes it sentimental, and 'truth' is a flat rendering of the Hebrew's sense of something that holds. The crux comes at the end. 'You have made great over all your name your word' can be read as KJV does ('magnified thy word above all thy name'), or with the nouns reversed (Radak, Meiri: your name above all your word). Rashi and Metzudat David read the name as the attributes of power and judgement, such as 'jealous and avenging', and the word as the promise of mercy that stands above them. The text says only that the word stands highest; the director should play it as astonishment that a promise outranks a name.

philological_notes.note: A poetic word for 'utterance, promise, saying'. Radak and Meiri read it as the promise made to David, which God kept and exceeded. Rashi reads it as the promise to be gracious.
Loyalty within a relationship that carries obligation, the opposite of a casual favour. Malbim distinguishes it from אֱמֶת, taking the first as the miraculous order and the second as the natural one.

verses.translation_literal: On the day I called, and you answered me; you made me bold in my soul, strength.
verses.translation_dramatic: On the very day I called, you answered. You did not keep me waiting. And something rose in me, in the deep place where I live: a boldness, a strength that was not mine until then.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse has the rhythm of an event: 'I called' and 'you answered' are two beats with no gap, and 'on the day' is a moment, not a season. The grammar after them is rough: תַּרְהִבֵנִי בְנַפְשִׁי עֹז, 'you make me bold in my soul strength', has two objects, the person and the strength (so Ibn Ezra). KJV's 'strengthenedst me with strength' is a fair version of the shape, but it hides the root.

The verb רָהַב is related to Rahab, the sea monster, and to rahab, 'arrogance'. Here it is positive: to make someone stout, swaggering, bold. Rashi glosses it as 'made me great'; Metzudat Zion as strengthening, comparing Ps 90:10. The נֶפֶשׁ ('soul') is the whole self: appetite, breath, life. KJV's 'soul' is right, but a modern reader hears 'soul' as only spiritual; the Hebrew means that David's whole being stood taller. Play it as a posture change: the man who called is not the man who stands.

philological_notes.note: A Hiphil with two objects: 'you make me bold, [with] strength'. The root can also mean arrogance, but here it is a gift. Rashi: 'you made me great'; Metzudat Zion: 'strengthening'.

verses.translation_literal: They will give thanks to you, YHWH, all the kings of the earth, for they have heard the words of your mouth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them come, O LORD: every king of the earth will give you thanks, for they have heard it, the words that came from your own mouth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse widens the stage sharply. The man who sang before the gods now sees the kings of the earth join him, and the cause is hearing. The commentaries split on what they heard. Radak, Meiri and Ibn Ezra say it was the promise of kingship to David, which the kings had given up on when they saw him hunted, and which God then kept. Rashi says the Ten Commandments at Sinai, beginning with 'I am' and 'you shall have no other gods' (Ex 20:2-3), accepting God's kingship before the decrees. Metzudat David says the word that God takes back those who return.

The verb is an imperfect, so 'will give thanks' or 'let them give thanks' fits; KJV's 'when they hear' turns the Hebrew 'for they have heard' into a future condition. The Hebrew perfect says the hearing has already happened, and the thanks follow from it. אִמְרֵי־פִיךָ, 'the words of your mouth', makes God a speaker with a mouth, in the royal image of a king whose decree is heard. The kings are the audience whom David had in view when he sang 'before gods' in verse 1.

philological_notes.note: 'The words of your mouth' is the plural of the same noun that appears as אִמְרָתֶךָ in verse 2. The commentators read it as the promise to David (Radak, Meiri) or as the Sinai commandments (Rashi).

verses.translation_literal: And they will sing in the ways of YHWH, for great [is] the glory of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: And they will sing, those kings of the earth, they will sing of the ways of the LORD, and the song will rise on the very roads he has walked. For great, great is the glory of the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The kings of verse 4 do not merely thank; they now break into song, and the verb carries on from the thanks: they have heard the words of YHWH's mouth, and the only fitting answer is a song. Court life in the ancient Near East was full of songs to a patron deity and to the king, and Egyptian and Mesopotamian rulers sang the praises of their own gods. Here foreign rulers sing in the ways of Israel's God.

The small preposition בְּ is the hinge. KJV and Webster have "in the ways of the Lord", YLT likewise, while ASV and BBE have "of" and "about". The Hebrew allows both: the kings sing *about* his ways, and they sing *within* them, walking his path as they sing. Ibn Ezra reads it as a contrast of kinds of song: not songs of desire or of war, but songs in the ways of the LORD that tell of his deeds. Metzudat David likewise says they will not sing songs of laughter and desire, but sing of the ways of the LORD, meaning the conduct of his attributes. Malbim has the kings sing because his glory depends on himself and is not diminished when he looks on the lowly. KJV's "Yea" softens a plain waw ("and"), and its "glory" is right: כָּבוֹד is the word for weight, what makes someone count. Targum has "they will praise" over "the paths of the LORD", rendering the ways as paths.

The verse closes with a repeated divine name, YHWH at the head of both halves, so that the song begins and ends on the name.

philological_notes.note: Imperfect third masculine plural of שיר, "to sing", with the conjunction. STEPBible reads "so they may sing" (purpose or result), but a simple continuing "and they will sing" fits the run of verse 4's future verbs. It names the act of song, not praise in general.
דֶּרֶךְ is a road or path, then the way someone acts. With בְּ it can mean the kings sing about YHWH's ways or sing while on them. Metzudat David takes the ways as the conduct of his attributes.
From the root "to be heavy": weight, substance, and so honor and glory. The cause of the song is that his weight is great, which Malbim reads as not depending on his regard for the lowly.

verses.translation_literal: For exalted is YHWH, and the lowly he sees, and the lofty from afar he knows.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD is high above all things, and yet it is the low he sees. The proud, the ones who stand tall in their own eyes, he knows only from far away.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse turns on a reversal of space. In every palace of the ancient Near East, the one who is near the king is the one who is high. Malbim's point is exactly this: with God the height is not rank, the lowly are close and the lofty are far. 'The lowly' (שָׁפָל) is the humble and the poor, and 'the lofty' (גָּבֹהַּ) is the proud, with the same root as height. The two adjectives are used without nouns, so the Hebrew says 'the low' and 'the high'.

KJV: 'Though the Lord be high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly'. The 'though ... yet' is an addition; the Hebrew has a simple 'and', which leaves the paradox for the listener to hear. 'Hath respect' is archaic for 'sees'. The last verb, יְיֵדָע, is odd in form. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Metzudat David connect it with וַיּוֹדַע in Judg 8:16, where Gideon 'taught' the men of Succoth with thorns, and read it as 'he disciplines the proud from afar'. Radak reads it as 'he makes known'. Most English versions read 'knows', which is the plain sense and is also the safer one. Ibn Ezra reads the whole verse as the poet's own history: he was a shepherd and God saw him.

philological_notes.note: An irregular form of ידע, with a doubled yod. The medieval commentators read it as the causative, 'he makes know, disciplines', as in Judg 8:16, and Ibn Ezra explains the form as the Hiphil with a guttural. The ordinary reading is 'he knows'.
'Low' in position and in rank. Used here as a noun, 'the lowly'. The opposite of גָּבֹהַּ ('high, proud').

verses.translation_literal: If I walk in the midst of trouble, you keep me alive; against the nose of my enemies you stretch out your hand, and your right hand saves me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even if I must walk through the very heart of trouble, you will keep me alive. When my enemies burn with fury, you reach out your hand against them, and your right hand brings me through.
verses.directors_commentary:
'If I walk in the midst of trouble' is not a hypothetical but a habit of mind: trouble is the road, and God is the one who keeps the traveller alive. בְּקֶרֶב is the inside of a thing, as the commentators say: not on the edge of trouble but deep within it, nearly to death (Radak, Meiri). The verb תְּחַיֵּנִי is the Piel of 'to live', so literally 'you make me live'. KJV's 'revive' is soft; the idea is preservation of life.

The Hebrew says 'against the אַף of my enemies'. אַף is the nose, and in Hebrew anger is the heavy breathing of an animal through flared nostrils; 'his nose burned' is the idiom for rage. KJV has 'wrath', which loses the physical picture. Ibn Ezra offers a second reading, 'in spite of their nose', that is, to enrage them, and Radak and Meiri say 'against their will'. In that sense the Targum has 'on the nostril of my enemies', and the English renders it as 'against the wrath'.

The two hands are God's: the one stretched out against the enemy and the right hand that saves. The right hand is the hand of power and favour, and in an army the place of the strongest. Malbim, reading the verse as justice and mercy at once, makes the stretched hand a hand of judgement.

philological_notes.note: The nose or nostril, and by extension anger, which in Hebrew is shown by the nose. The phrase עַל־אַף means 'against the anger of', and in its literal sense something like 'to their noses'. Ibn Ezra also reads it as 'to spite them'.
The Piel of 'to live': you cause me to live, you keep me alive. Metzudat David reads it as 'from the trouble', that is, bringing me through it.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH will complete on my behalf. YHWH, your covenant loyalty is for ever; the works of your hands, do not let go.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD will finish what he has begun for me. O LORD, your steadfast love does not end, it lasts for ever. Do not let go of what your own hands have made.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a pivot from statement to plea. The first clause is a flat declaration, 'YHWH will complete on my behalf', and then the voice turns and speaks to God by name: 'YHWH, your loyalty is for ever'. The final line is an imperative with no softening: 'do not let go'. The three clauses move from certainty to petition in one breath, and the actor should drop the volume at the end.

KJV: 'will perfect that which concerneth me'. 'Perfect' is the Latin sense of 'complete', and the Hebrew גמר does mean to finish, to bring to completion (Metzudat Zion; Radak: 'as he began to be good to me, so he will finish'). Meiri, Radak and Metzudat David read the phrase as God completing the promise already begun. The STEPBible gloss 'avenge' is not the sense; the Targum, though, reads it as 'will complete evil upon them'. 'That which concerneth me' translates בַּעֲדִי, 'on my behalf, for my sake'.

'Forsake not' is KJV for אַל־תֶּרֶף, whose root means to sag or let go slack (compare Deut 31:6, 'he will not let you go', which Meiri cites). 'The works of your hands' is the language of a craftsman and his work: David is a thing that God made and raised up (Radak), and Rashi reads 'the works of your hands' as the temple, built by God's hands (Ex 15:17). A potter does not smash his own pot.

philological_notes.note: To bring to an end, complete, finish. STEPBible's 'he will avenge' is not supported by the verb; the sense is that God will bring to completion what he began. Metzudat Zion: 'from the sense of finishing and completing'.
To sink, slacken, let go, in the Hiphil jussive: 'do not let your hand sag'. Meiri compares Deut 31:6 ('he will not fail you nor forsake you'); Metzudat Zion links it to the sense of slackness.
